steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Jihad means "struggle" or "striving" — NOT "holy war." There are two types: the greater jihad (internal spiritual struggle against sin) and the lesser jihad (external struggle, which may include armed combat under strict conditions).

steps.title: Exam Tip
steps.body: The vast majority of Muslims interpret jihad primarily as the greater jihad — the inner struggle. Terrorist attacks that kill civilians violate every condition of lesser jihad and are condemned by mainstream Islamic scholars.

steps.title: RS Exam Tips — Jihad
steps.body: 1. For Jihad questions, always include specific scriptural or source references where relevant 2. Explain both religious and non-religious viewpoints 3. Use specialist vocabulary precisely (e.g. terms from the specification) 4. Evaluate by analysing strengths and weaknesses of different views before reaching your conclusion 5. Link your discussion of Jihad to its real-world impact on believers and society

steps.title: UK Context
steps.body: A British Muslim student who refuses to join friends in drinking alcohol, who fasts during Ramadan while sitting in the school canteen, and who maintains their five daily prayers despite exam stress, is practising greater jihad. These everyday acts of faithfulness require courage and self-discipline.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Explain the difference between greater and lesser jihad.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always refer to specific sources of authority (scripture, sacred texts, religious leaders) Explain contrasting beliefs — different views within and between traditions Use key terminology precisely (e.g. tawhid, atonement, sanctity of life) For 12-mark evaluation questions, consider both sides before reaching a justified conclusion Link beliefs to their impact on individuals, communities and society Acknowledge diversity — no religious tradition has a single, uniform view
